Graph-theory based analyses of human motor 
learning: A resting-state fMRI study
1st Shahryar Ebrahimi
2nd Fariba Bahrami
3rd Gholam-Ali Hossein-Zadeh
2019 26th National and 4th International Iranian Conference on Biomedical Engineering (ICBME),
Iran University of Science and Technology (IUST), Tehran, Iran, 27-28 November 2019
Abstract—Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging
(rs-fMRI) is a promising method to investigate brain functional
connectivity (FC) changes resulted from interventional studies.
Graph-theory based analyses quantify multiple aspects of the
brain network by computing different metrics. We used a graph￾theory approach to investigate neural plasticity of the human
brain due to a novel motor learning protocol that has not been
addressed before using rs-fMRI. Thirteen young and healthy
participants practiced seven sessions of motor learning exercises.
rs-fMRI data were collected before the first and after the 7th
session of exercises. We performed ROI-to-ROI analyses along
with the computation of different graph metrics on rs-fMRI data
after preprocessing steps. The graph networks were constructed
using correlation signals originating from 164 parcellated regions
(Harvard-Oxford atlas) of the brain. In further analyses, different
metrics of the constructed graph were computed and compared
between pre- and post-training sessions using proper statistical
tests. Thirteen significant regions of interest (Left Dorsal At￾tention.IPS, Left Angular Gyrus, and Right Postcentral Gyrus,
to name a few) were obtained with p-FDR < 0.05, which had
essential roles in the motor learning procedure.

Thirteen young, healthy subjects (six female and seven 
male, mean aged = 23 ± 3.37 years, two left-footed and 11 
right-footed) without any neurological or psychiatric disorder 
participated in our study. All of the subjects confirmed their 
consent by filling special forms in the Iranian National Brain 
Mapping Laboratory (NBML), Tehran, Iran. Also, the Re￾search Ethics Committee of Iran University of Medical Science 
(IUMS) approved the experimental protocol.

The dataset was acquired in NBML. Each subject 
underwent two 10-minutes rs-fMRI data acquisition and 
seven motor training sessions every other day, according to 
the block diagram of Fig. 1. Subjects were told to keep their
eyes open and try to stay in a relaxed position under the MRI 
scanner. One of the data acquisition sessions was held before 
the training sessions (Pre-training) and the other after them 
(Post-training). Before the training sessions, subjects were 
completely informed of what they were going to do in the 
experiments. All training sessions were the same except for 
the first (Day 1) and last (Day 7) sessions, which included 
one more item. During the training sessions, subjects were 
sitting on a seat, and a digital pen was attached to the 
inner side of their dominant foot. The exact 
place of pen attachment was the junction of metatarsal and 
phalanges in the human foot bones. The pen was firmly fixed 
in place with the help of special belts and adhesive tapes. 
There was a large digital tablet under the foot of subjects, 
and they were able to draw whatever they desired. 
Besides, a 15-inch Lenovo laptop was placed in 
front of them, and they needed to follow the motor learning 
procedure according to the guides displayed on the screen.
Generally, subjects had to draw some specific 
shapes with the digital pen by controlling their foot.
Each training session lasted approximately 30 minutes. It 
consisted of five trials, each with a 100-second rest period. 
The protocol of each session was as follows, and the subjects 
were asked to have a trade-off between accuracy and speed 
of drawing. They couldn't see the location of the digital pen, 
but their drawings were displayed on the screen in a real-time 
manner.
Displaying a sequence of repetitive spiral shapes on the 
screen (only at the beginning of Day 1 and at the end of 
Day 7). Subjects had to draw their spirals between the 
lines of the displayed one.
Displaying a set of dots on the perimeter and center of 
a circle (reach-out shape). Subjects had to draw lines 
from the center dot, reaching out to the dots on the circle 
perimeter in the beginning of each trial of
Day 1 to Day 7.
Displaying a specific set of boundary shapes in a random 
order (one trial). Each shape of the set repeated only 
once during a trial. The space between the sides of each 
boundary shape was set to 2cm. Subjects had to draw 
inside the boundary of each shape, starting from the 
lower-left corner, and only had 15 seconds to rest between 
trials.

Siemens Prisma 3.0T MRI scanner was used to acquire 
structural and rs-fMRI images. A magnetization prepared rapid 
acquisition gradient echo (MP-RAGE) pulse sequence (TR = 
1800, TE = 3.62, TI = 1100, flip angle = 7) was implemented 
to acquire a High-resolution structural volume of the subjects 
with 160 sagittal slices, each 1mm thick with 0.85 x 0.85 mm2 
in-plane resolution. In addition, echo-planar imaging (EPI) 
pulse sequence was used (TR = 2000, TE = 30, flip angle = 90) 
to acquire 34 transverse slices covering the whole brain, each 
3mm thick with a 64 x 64 matrix and an in-plane resolution 
of 3 x 3 mm2.

All preprocessing steps were carried out using CONN 
v.18b (http://www.nitrc.org/projects/conn) and SPM12 
(https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12) functional 
connectivity toolboxes as follows: After initial removal of 
first five volumes for stabilization of hemodynamic response 
function (HRF) signal, voxel displacement maps (VDMs) were 
created to undistort EPI images. Then, resting-state data were 
realigned to their initial volume, corrected for slice timing, 
and scrubbed with an intermediate criteria in which, if the 
global signal difference of two subsequent volumes exceeded 
the z-value of 9 or relative motion of them exceeded 3mm, 
the corresponding volumes were labeled, and their effects 
were regressed out of the voxels'signal. Also, resting-state
data were co-registered to the corresponding structural images, 
resampled to 3 x 3 x 3 mm3, normalized to the standard MNI 
atlas, and smoothed with a 5mm FWHM Gaussian kernel. 
Further preprocessing steps consisted of nuisance covariates 
regression and band-pass filtering (0.01-0.08 Hz) to eliminate 
the effects of physiological artifacts on graph-based analyses. 
Six motion parameters plus their first derivatives, five 
principal components from white matter and SCF (obtained 
using CompCor algorithm) along with a linear de-trending 
term integrated a total of 23 regressors for nuisance covariates 
regression step.

Data of subject 4 from pre-training and subject 1 from 
post-training rs-fMRI sessions were discarded due to the high 
amount of absolute motions. We employed the Harvard-Oxford 
(HO) atlas to percellate the brain into 164 independent regions 
of interest (ROIs). Time-series of the voxels within each of the 
ROIs were averaged to gain a representative signal for each. To 
construct a dense, complex network of the brain, the FC matrix 
was calculated among each pair of the ROIs using correlation. 
The functional connectivity matrix has 13,366 undirected 
weighted edges. We thresholded the functional connectivity 
matrix using a proportional thresholding procedure rather than 
setting a typical threshold on the correlation (r) itself. 
This analysis maximizes the global cost-efficiency (GCE), which is defined as the 
global efficiency at a given cost minus the cost, (i.e., GCE 
= GE - C). The cost in which GCE has its maximum value 
(Cmax) is chosen to threshold the connectivity matrix. In this 
way, Cmax percent of the whole edges that have the most 
reliable correlation values remain, and the others are set to 
zero for each subject. All self-connections (diagonal weights 
of functional connectivity matrix) are also set to zero. 
Two measures of functional segregation (clustering 
coefficient and local efficiency), three functional 
integration measures (average path length, cost, and 
global efficiency), and two local nodal measures (degree 
and betweenness centrality) were computed based on 
the thresholded and weighted functional connectivity matrix 
using CONN v.18b. 
We performed two kinds of analysis based on the brain’s 
network graph. All graph metrics were compared to each other 
across the pre- and post-training sessions in all of the 164 
ROIs by performing proper statistical tests and defining post 
> pre contrast. The computed graph metrics for both pre- and 
post-training sessions were 12-element sets of numbers (one 
subject removed from each session) in all of the ROIs. To 
check the mean differences of the sets, a two-tale paired t-test 
was performed. Significant changes of metrics in ROIs were 
detected, and the resulting ROIs were addressed in 
further analyses, which compared the connection strength of 
the selected ROIs between the pre- and post-training sessions 
and themselves (obtained ROIs x pre-post training interactions) 
by implementing an F-test.

Comparing the drawings of Day 1 to Day 7 revealed a 
significant visual alteration in motor control of the subjects. As 
it is obvious in the drawings the drawings have been converged into 
a more regular pattern across the subjects.
